title: Do shoppers prefer a chatbot when buying embarrassing products? What a Journal of Consumer Psychology study found

<p class="mw-kicker">Marketing in 3 · <a href="../../2024/index.html">2024 in research</a> · No. 7 · Paper published 14 February 2024</p>
<figure class="mw-hero"><picture><source type="image/webp" sizes="(max-width: 900px) 100vw, 900px" srcset="../../images/web/2024-chatbot-embarrassment-960.webp 960w, ../../images/web/2024-chatbot-embarrassment-1600.webp 1600w"><img src="../../images/2024-chatbot-embarrassment.jpg" alt="A person in a blue velvet jacket holds an empty pink hand-mirror frame in front of their face, against a blue roller shutter" width="1600" height="900" fetchpriority="high" decoding="async"></picture><figcaption>Some questions are easier to ask when nobody is looking back. Photo: Edgar Nunley on Unsplash.</figcaption></figure>
<section class="mw-answer" aria-label="Short answer"><h2>The short answer</h2><div class="mw-ans-grid"><p>Often, yes, if the bot is plainly labelled and does not act human. In an experiment where more than 1,300 Americans imagined buying diarrhoea medicine online, people were readier to chat with an agent that said it was a bot than with a human service rep. Give that bot a cartoon face and gushing lines and its edge largely vanished. And when nobody says who is typing, shoppers with something to hide tend to assume a person is.</p><div class="mw-ev" role="note" aria-label="Evidence level: 2 of 3 stars, several studies"><span class="ev-k">Evidence level</span><ol><li><span class="ev-s" aria-hidden="true"><b>★</b><i>★</i><i>★</i></span>One study</li><li class="on"><span class="ev-s" aria-hidden="true"><b>★</b><b>★</b><i>★</i></span>Several studies</li><li><span class="ev-s" aria-hidden="true"><b>★</b><b>★</b><b>★</b></span>Meta-analysis</li></ol></div></div></section>
<section class="mw-takeaways"><h2>Key takeaways</h2><ul><li>Buying hay fever tablets, 91% of students picked the online pharmacy with a human adviser over one run by a chatbot. Switch the purchase to antidiarrhoeal medicine and the chatbot shop gained ground, with awkwardness showing up in people&#x27;s written reasons.</li><li>In a live skincare chat, 119 of the 191 people who handed over an email address for a free sample had been talking to a labelled bot; only 72 had been talking to a supposed person.</li><li>A cartoon face and an excited tone made a labelled bot seem far more able to feel: 2.77 against 1.79 for a plain speech-bubble bot, with a human rep at 3.61.</li><li>For the 14.5% of people most uneasy talking about sex, a humanlike bot that openly called itself a bot was credited with roughly as much inner life as a human agent.</li></ul></section>
<section id="what-the-researchers-did"><h2>What the researchers did</h2><p><a class="mw-orcid-link" href="https://orcid.org/0000-0002-8682-4697" title="Jianna Jin on ORCID">Jianna Jin</a>, Jesse Walker and <a class="mw-orcid-link" href="https://orcid.org/0000-0003-1127-5272" title="Rebecca Walker Reczek on ORCID">Rebecca Walker Reczek</a>, all of the Fisher College of Business at The Ohio State University
in Columbus, started from something that sets chatbots apart from service robots. A robot in a shop is obviously a
robot. The agent in a chat window could be a program or a person, and many firms never say which.</p><p>Their question was what happens when the purchase is a little mortifying. Earlier work on embarrassment
mostly looked at shops, where other customers and staff can see what you buy. Here the worry is more private: picturing
someone on the other end of the chat reading your question, even while you sit alone at home.</p><p>They ran six studies with products chosen to make people self-conscious: personal lubricant, antidiarrhoeal
medicine and skincare, set against harmless comparisons such as body lotion and hay fever tablets. Sometimes nobody
said what the agent was. Other times it was spelled out, and the bot either looked plain or was dressed up to seem
human.</p>
<dl class="mw-facts"><div><dt>Studies 1 and 2</dt><dd>403 US online panel members, then 795 US women, all meeting an agent whose identity was never stated</dd></div><div><dt>Study 3</dt><dd>1,501 US adults recruited, 1,316 kept after a preregistered check that they knew which agent they had met</dd></div><div><dt>Study 4</dt><dd>600 US adults judging a humanlike but clearly labelled bot or a human rep</dd></div><div><dt>Studies 5a and 5b</dt><dd>386 undergraduates choosing between two online pharmacies; 595 US adults in a live, scripted skincare chat</dd></div><div><dt>Agents</dt><dd>A plain bot (speech-bubble picture), a bot with a cartoon woman&#x27;s picture and emotional language, or a rep with a real photo</dd></div><div><dt>Open data</dt><dd>Materials, data and preregistrations posted on the Open Science Framework</dd></div></dl>
</section>
<section id="when-the-chat-could-be-a-person-or-a-program"><h2>When the chat could be a person or a program</h2><p>In the first two studies, shoppers saw a chat window with a photo of a real woman asking about their preferences.
Nothing said whether someone or some software sat behind it.</p><p>In Study 1, people imagined looking for lubricant on a store&#x27;s website and then guessed who they were chatting with.
The more uncomfortable someone felt discussing sex, the more likely they were to say a person was typing. Study 2
switched the product rather than measuring discomfort. Women shown the identical store and chat rated the chance of
a human agent at 4.01 out of 9 when the shelves held lubricant, and 3.68 when they held body lotion.</p><p>The explanation comes from error management theory: when unsure, people drift towards the mistake that would hurt
less. Assuming you face a bot and then learning a person read your question is the costlier error. So the shoppers who
feel most exposed assume a human and brace themselves, or skip the chat altogether, and never get the ease a bot
could have given them.</p>
</section>
<section id="a-labelled-bot-wins-a-humanlike-one-does-not"><h2>A labelled bot wins, a humanlike one does not</h2><p>Study 3 made the agent&#x27;s identity explicit. People imagined buying antidiarrhoeal medicine from an online drugstore
and met one of three agents: a bot called S.A.M. with a speech-bubble icon, a bot that also declared itself a bot but
had a cartoon woman as its picture and greeted people with excited, emotional lines, or a human rep called Sam with
a real photo.</p><p>The plain bot came out on top. The friendlier, more lifelike bot, despite openly saying what it was, scored below
the plain one and could not be told apart from the human rep on willingness to chat.</p><p>A follow-up with 300 people showed why. Both bots seemed equally able to remember, plan and communicate. What changed
was how much feeling people credited them with. Study 4 then found that people most uncomfortable discussing sex saw
more inner life in a humanlike labelled bot, while their discomfort left their view of a human rep unchanged. A
further test with a plain bot found no such pattern. Human touches leave room for worried shoppers to imagine the bot
noticing what they buy.</p>

</section>
<section id="from-comfort-to-sign-ups"><h2>From comfort to sign-ups</h2><p>Study 5a moved from chatting to choosing a shop. Undergraduates picked between two online pharmacies, one where a
chatbot gave advice and one with a human service agent. Two independent coders, blind to the hypotheses, rated
each person&#x27;s written reason for their choice. Those buying antidiarrhoeal medicine mentioned awkwardness more
(1.38 against 1.06 on a five-point coding scale), and that awkwardness explained the shift in which pharmacy they
chose.</p><p>Study 5b used a real conversation. Americans who care about how their skin looks joined a trial session for a
skincare brand. One group chatted with an agent labelled &quot;Chatbot&quot; that replied instantly; the other chatted with &quot;Sam&quot;,
shown with a photo of a woman and slower to answer. Both were the same program asking the same questions, ending
with an offer of a free sample in exchange for an email address.</p><p>People rated the labelled bot as far less able to feel (2.34 against 3.60). That lowered their embarrassment, which
in turn made them readier to share an address. How capable of thinking and planning the agent seemed made no difference
to that chain.</p>

<section id="why-managers-may-miss-this"><h2>Why managers may miss this</h2><p>A further preregistered study of 816 Americans, reported in the online appendix, described a dating service whose
agent asks about dating and sexual history. People chose the bot more often for themselves than when asked what the
average customer would pick. We tend to underrate how awkward other people feel, and the authors suspect managers do
the same when they decide who staffs the chat.</p><p>Their advice is specific. Where a purchase can make people self-conscious, say clearly that the agent is a bot and
keep it plain. Where it cannot, most shoppers still lean towards a person. The authors also float ideas they did not
test: people who feel they know too little about a product, people facing a stereotype about their group, or people
applying for stigmatised services such as welfare might also prefer an honest bot. A bot that drops even its
first-person voice could do better still.</p>
</section>
<section id="how-to-apply-it" class="mw-howto"><p class="mw-rsg-kicker">Marketing in 3 steps</p><h2>Ready. Set. Market.</h2><div class="mw-rsg"><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">1</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Ready</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Decide and prepare</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Mark the awkward products.</strong> Go through your catalogue and flag every product or service people might hesitate to ask about in person, such as bowel trouble, intimate health, hair loss, skin problems or debt. Aim for a working list of ten to twenty items.</li><li><strong>Decide who answers where.</strong> Route chat on those flagged pages to an automated assistant. Keep a person on chat for everyday products, where most shoppers would rather talk to someone real.</li></ul></div><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">2</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Set</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Build it</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Say it is a bot straight away.</strong> Put the word &quot;automated&quot; or &quot;bot&quot; in the chat header. Make the first line say it plainly, for example: &quot;You&#x27;re chatting with an automated assistant.&quot; Nobody should have to guess.</li><li><strong>Strip out the human touches.</strong> Swap any face or cartoon person for a plain logo or symbol. Give the assistant a functional name rather than a first name, and cut exclamation marks, emojis and gushing phrases from the script.</li></ul></div><div class="mw-phase"><div class="mw-phase-dot" aria-hidden="true">3</div><div class="mw-phase-tag"><span class="mw-phase-name">Market</span><span class="mw-phase-sub">Launch and measure</span></div><ul class="mw-rsg-steps"><li><strong>Offer a discreet next step.</strong> End each sensitive chat with something useful the shopper can take away discreetly, such as a trial size or a short guide sent by email under a neutral subject line.</li><li><strong>Compare for four weeks.</strong> Run the labelled, plain assistant on half of the flagged pages and your current set-up on the rest for four weeks. Count chats started, questions answered and email addresses collected on each side.</li></ul></div></div></section>

<section id="what-to-expect"><h2>What to expect</h2><ul class="mw-list"><li><strong>Less awkwardness, not none.</strong> Even with the labelled bot, embarrassment fell only from 2.53 to 2.22 out of seven. Most people were not mortified to begin with; the bot takes the edge off.</li><li><strong>Fuller answers.</strong> Shoppers volunteered a little more to the bot in a product-finder chat, which can make its recommendations better matched to what they need.</li><li><strong>People still win for everyday items.</strong> The bot&#x27;s advantage only shows up when a purchase stirs worry about how one looks to others. For ordinary products, keep humans available.</li><li><strong>Disclosure and marketing can point the same way.</strong> A 2018 California law, cited in the paper, already obliges automated online agents to say what they are. For sensitive ranges, being upfront is not just compliance but an advantage.</li></ul></section>
<section id="where-it-does-not-work"><h2>Where it does not work</h2><ul class="mw-list"><li><strong>Mostly imagined shopping.</strong> Five of the six studies used screenshots and scenarios. Only one involved a live chat, and even there the human was a scripted program.</li><li><strong>American panels and students.</strong> Most people came from Amazon Mechanical Turk, plus one group of undergraduates. Cultures with different norms about bodily topics may react differently.</li><li><strong>The fake human behaved a little differently.</strong> In the live chat, &quot;Sam&quot; replied more slowly and allowed free typing for the opening reply. A post-test found people did see Sam as more likely to be a person, and the chat felt just as easy and smooth, but the authors still list this as a weakness.</li><li><strong>Sign-ups, not sales.</strong> Nobody bought anything. The closest thing to real behaviour was handing over an email address, and the paper reports how those sign-ups split between the two agents rather than the sign-up rate in each group.</li><li><strong>Small shifts in guessing.</strong> The tilt towards assuming a human, when identity was left open, was modest in size.</li></ul></section>
<section id="questions"><h2>Questions marketers ask</h2><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Do customers prefer chatbots or human agents?</h3><p>It depends on the purchase. For everyday products most people lean towards a person. When a purchase could make them self-conscious, a clearly labelled, plainly designed bot made shoppers more willing to ask for help than a human agent did (Jin et al., 2025).</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Should a chatbot tell customers it is a bot?</h3><p>For sensitive purchases, yes. Left to guess, the shoppers most worried about being judged tended to assume a person was on the other end, which wiped out the relief a bot might have given.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Is it a good idea to make a chatbot seem human?</h3><p>Not where embarrassment is in play. A cartoon face and emotional language led people to credit the bot with feelings, after which it lost its lead over a human rep in getting shoppers to keep chatting.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Why is a bot less embarrassing than a person?</h3><p>Because people doubt it can feel or judge. In these studies it was the bot&#x27;s perceived lack of emotions and awareness, not its ability to think or plan, that lowered embarrassment.</p></div><div class="mw-faq"><h3>Which products count as embarrassing?</h3><p>Here the test products were linked to sex, stomach upsets and how one&#x27;s skin looks. Anything tied to bodily functions, sex or appearance can qualify, and the authors suggest that lack of know-how or a stigmatised service could trigger the same worry.</p></div></section>
<section id="also-new"><h2>Also new at the time</h2><div class="mw-also"><article><p class="mw-also-src"><em>Journal of Interactive Marketing</em> · 2024</p><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/10949968231221472">Showing or Hiding? The Impact of Visibility of General Conditions of Use on Retargeted Ad Intrusiveness and Perceived Ethicality of Mobile Apps</a></h3><p class="mw-also-au">Toti &amp; Steils</p><p>Across seven studies, app users met retargeted ads after terms of use that had been either prominent or tucked away. When the conditions were easy to see, people held the company less to blame for the ads and saw themselves as having agreed to them, so the ads felt less pushy and the firm seemed more ethical. How much people worried about privacy, and whether the app later reminded them what they had accepted, changed the strength of that effect. Fine print seems to work better as large print.</p></article><article><p class="mw-also-src"><em>Psychology &amp; Marketing</em> · 2024</p><h3><a href="https://doi.org/10.1002/mar.21982">Using large language models to generate silicon samples in consumer and marketing research: Challenges, opportunities, and guidelines</a></h3><p class="mw-also-au">Sarstedt et al.</p><p>Can a language model stand in for survey respondents? This review gathers the studies that compared answers from GPT-style &quot;silicon samples&quot; with answers from real people and finds the match swings widely from one topic to the next. The authors see the safest use early in a project, for pretesting questions and trying out designs, and set stricter conditions and ethical cautions for synthetic answers in main studies. A model can be a sparring partner for your questionnaire, but it is not yet your customer.</p></article></div></section>
